passages.happening:
Moses calls Bezalel, Oholiab and every skilled person, and hands them the gifts the people have brought (verses 2-3). “Meanwhile, the people continued to bring freewill offerings morning after morning” (verse 3).

The craftsmen leave their work to tell Moses, “The people are bringing more than enough for doing the work the LORD has commanded us to do” (verse 5).

So word goes through the camp: “No man or woman should make anything else as an offering for the sanctuary” (verse 6). “So the people were restrained from bringing more, since what they already had was more than enough to perform all the work” (verses 6-7).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 35 called for gifts and workers. Chapter 36 shows both at work, and it opens with one of the most surprising scenes in the Bible. A people has to be told to stop giving.

Only a few chapters back, these same people poured their gold into an idol. Now they bring gifts ‘morning after morning’, until the workers themselves say it is too much. The Hebrew word for ‘enough’ is said twice. It marks a rare moment in Scripture, when God's people give beyond what is needed.

Notice two honest things in the scene. The craftsmen do not keep the extra. They report it. And Moses does not go on collecting. When the need is met, he says so, and the giving stops.

Forgiven people give like this. Nothing in the chapter says they were pressed or shamed into it. The calf was made on demand. The tabernacle is built from gifts that had to be held back.
passages.later:
Paul saw the same thing in the poor churches of Macedonia: “they gave according to their ability and even beyond it. Of their own accord, they earnestly pleaded with us for the privilege of sharing in this service to the saints” (2 Corinthians 8:3-4).

He thanked the Philippians for a gift that did the same: “I have all I need and more, now that I have received your gifts” (Philippians 4:18).
passages.asks: The people gave until they were told to stop. Ask when you last gave, in money, time or care, beyond what was asked. And ask whether, like Moses and the craftsmen, you are honest about what you have been given and what is truly needed.

passages.happening:
“All the skilled craftsmen among the workmen made the ten curtains for the tabernacle. They were made of finely spun linen, as well as blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, with cherubim skillfully worked into them” (verse 8). They are joined with loops of blue and fifty gold clasps, “so that the tabernacle was a unit” (verses 10-13).

Then come the curtains of goat hair for the tent over the tabernacle, joined with bronze clasps (verses 14-18). “Additionally, he made for the tent a covering of ram skins dyed red, and over that a covering of fine leather” (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
From here the chapter follows 26:1-37 almost phrase for phrase. In chapter 26 God said what was to be made. Here the text says ‘he made’, again and again. The one who makes is Bezalel, with those he leads. Command has become deed.

The order is different from the plans. The plans began with the ark, at the center, and worked outward. The builders begin with the tent, the house itself, and make the furniture afterward.

The note on chapter 26 describes the layers. The innermost is fine linen in blue, purple and scarlet, with cherubim worked into it. Over that comes a tent of goat hair, then ram skins dyed red, then leather. From outside it was a plain tent. Its beauty was within, where the priests would see the cherubim all around and above them.

The numbers are repeated with care: fifty loops, fifty clasps, eleven curtains. Nothing is left to guesswork, and nothing is made up by the builders. After the calf, that exactness is the point.
passages.later:
Hebrews recalls the warning Moses was given before he built: “See to it that you make everything according to the pattern shown you on the mountain” (Hebrews 8:5).

Paul uses the picture of a building fitted together for the church: “In Him the whole building is fitted together and grows into a holy temple in the Lord” (Ephesians 2:21).
passages.asks: The builders made each curtain exactly as God had said. Ask where you are tempted to improve on what God has asked and do it your own way. And ask whether you can do careful, hidden work that no one outside will ever see.

passages.happening:
“Next, he constructed upright frames of acacia wood for the tabernacle. Each frame was ten cubits long and a cubit and a half wide” (verses 20-21). There are twenty for the south side, twenty for the north, and eight for the west, each standing on two silver bases (verses 23-30).

Crossbars of acacia wood hold the frames together (verses 31-33). “And he overlaid the frames with gold and made gold rings to hold the crossbars. He also overlaid the crossbars with gold” (verse 34).
passages.hearers:
The frames are the walls. Together they make a room usually pictured as about thirty cubits long and ten wide and high, roughly 45 by 15 by 15 feet. A cubit was about 18 inches, the length of a forearm.

The Hebrew word for the upright pieces may mean solid boards. Many interpreters think open frames are meant, since forty-eight solid planks of that size would have been very heavy to carry through the wilderness.

The rear of the tent is the west side. So the tent opened to the east.

The metals rise in value toward the center, as the note on chapter 26 explains: bronze at the entrance, silver under the walls, gold within. Every step inward was a step nearer to God.

The silver bases have a story of their own. They were cast from the half shekel that every man gave at the census (30:11-16; 38:27). The walls of God's house stood on the ransom silver of the whole people.
passages.later:
Exodus itself gives the account: “The hundred talents of silver were used to cast the bases of the sanctuary and the bases of the veil” (Exodus 38:27).

Peter says what believers were ransomed with: “not with perishable things such as silver or gold” (1 Peter 1:18), “but with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:19).
passages.hard:
Could a tent like this really have been built and carried in the wilderness?

Scholars disagree. In the nineteenth century Julius Wellhausen argued that the tabernacle never existed, and that priestly writers set a movable copy of Solomon's temple back in the time of Moses. Many critical scholars still hold some form of that view. They point to the rich materials and to how closely the plan matches the temple.

Others argue for a real sanctuary in the wilderness. They point to Egypt, where a gold-covered wooden frame that could be taken apart was found in the tomb of Queen Hetepheres, and where carvings of the camp of Ramesses II at Kadesh show the king's tent inside a rectangular enclosure. They point to the wealth Israel carried out of Egypt (12:35-36), and to the fact that the tabernacle's features fit a tent that travels better than a temple of stone.

Some take a middle view: a simpler tent of meeting existed (33:7-11), and the account describes it in ideal detail.

These notes take no side. Readers who differ here agree on what the text teaches. God chose to live among his people, and he did so on his own terms, in a house built to his design.
passages.asks: God's house stood on bases made from the ransom of every person, rich and poor alike. Ask what your life with God stands on. And ask whether you believe you have a place in what God is building, whatever you were able to bring.

passages.happening:
“Next, he made the veil of blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and finely spun linen, with cherubim skillfully worked into it” (verse 35). It hangs on four posts of acacia wood overlaid with gold, set in silver bases (verse 36).

“For the entrance to the tent, he made a curtain embroidered with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and finely spun linen” (verse 37), with five posts and bases of bronze (verse 38).
passages.hearers:
Two curtains close the tent. One hangs at the entrance. The other, the veil, hangs inside and divides the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place, where the ark will stand.

Cherubim are woven into the veil. In the Bible cherubim are not the plump infants of later art. They are mighty winged guardians. Similar creatures stood beside the thrones and palace doors of ancient kings. After Eden, cherubim guarded the way to the tree of life, on the east side of the garden. The tabernacle too opens to the east, and a veil with cherubim on it bars the way to the inner room.

So the tent says two things at once. God has come to live among his people. And the way into his presence is guarded and holy. Only the high priest would pass the veil, once a year, on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16).

The note on 26:31-37 says more about the veil, and about how it protected those who served near it.
passages.later:
Genesis tells of the first guarded way: God “stationed cherubim on the east side of the Garden of Eden, along with a whirling sword of flame to guard the way to the tree of life” (Genesis 3:24).

When Jesus died, “the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom” (Mark 15:38). Hebrews draws the meaning: “we have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way opened for us through the curtain of His body” (Hebrews 10:19-20).

That line is the New Testament's own. It does not make Israel's worship empty. As the notes on Hebrews 8 say, a shadow is real, and God truly met his people in this tent.
passages.asks: The veil guarded the way to God, and the New Testament says the way has been opened. Ask whether you come to God with confidence, or hang back as if the veil still hung there. And ask whether confidence has made you careless about his holiness.
